topicName: Architectural Decision Records (ADRs) and Documentation Culture
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Architectural Decision Records (ADRs) and Documentation Culture"},{"order":2,"type":"subheading","text":"Introduction to ADRs"},{"order":3,"type":"paragraph","text":"In fast-paced engineering teams, architectural decisions are frequently made during meetings, Slack chats, or pull request reviews. Without a centralized method to capture the context and consequences of these choices, teams often suffer from institutional amnesia. Architectural Decision Records (ADRs) provide a lightweight, immutable log of important architectural decisions, ensuring that the "why" behind a system design remains transparent to current and future engineers."},{"order":4,"type":"subheading","text":"What is an Architectural Decision Record?"},{"order":5,"type":"paragraph","text":"An ADR is a short text document that captures a single architectural decision, its context, and its consequences. Stored directly alongside the codebase (often in a docs/adr directory), ADRs leverage the same version control workflows as the application code itself."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Immutable: Once a decision is accepted, the record is never modified. If circumstances change, a new ADR is created to supersede the old one."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Contextual: Focuses heavily on the forces and constraints driving the decision at that specific point in time."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Transparent: Accessible to all team members, cross-functional partners, and onboarding engineers."},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"Standard Structure of an ADR"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Most ADRs follow a standardized template popularized by Michael Nygard. A typical template includes a Title, Status, Context, Decision, and Consequences."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"# 1. Record Kafka as the primary event bus

## Status
Accepted (2023-10-25)

## Context
Our microservices architecture requires asynchronous communication with high throughput and reliable event replay capabilities. RabbitMQ struggled with heavy load during peak traffic tests.

## Decision
We will adopt Apache Kafka as the enterprise event bus for all core domain events.

## Consequences
- Positive: High throughput, excellent event retention and replay.
- Negative: Increased operational complexity and infrastructure costs."},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Fostering a Documentation Culture"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Writing ADRs is not just about tools; it is about cultivating a culture of proactive communication. Engineering leaders must lower the friction of writing documentation and integrate it into the standard definition of done."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Treat ADRs as Code: Require an ADR in the pull request for any major architectural shift."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Keep Templates Simple: Use command-line tools like Log4Brains or ADR Tools to generate markdown files instantly."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Review During Onboarding: Use ADR reading as part of the new engineer onboarding process to accelerate their understanding of system constraints."},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"Adopting ADRs transforms how teams communicate technical tradeoffs. By shifting documentation from an afterthought to an active part of the design phase, you protect your team from recurring debates and build a resilient, understandable software architecture."}]
